title: The mark is not the author
summary: Anthropic's content-marking plan separates text watermarks from signed file provenance while leaving authorship and negative detection unresolved. Docker's five-layer sandbox model exposes the live workspace and host integrations that isolation does not automatically protect, and OpenAI's Texas infrastructure promises meet the harder question of project-level measurement and enforcement.

threads.name: Data-center buildout backlash
threads.status: OpenAI has answered Texas's emerging data-center standards with public commitments to fund project-driven infrastructure, support new generation, minimize water use, manage local impacts, and disclose resource and incentive information; project-specific metrics and enforcement remain to be shown.
threads.arc: The thread moves from Texas auditing the interconnection queue to a major AI developer accepting the state's accounting categories in public, with the next test shifting to permits, contracts, meters, and disclosures for a named project.

dives.why_it_matters: Publishers, compliance teams, educators, and people editing mixed human-machine drafts need to distinguish evidence that Claude processed content from claims about authorship, accuracy, ownership, or complete provenance.

Developers running coding agents unattended need to know which layer protects the host, project, credentials, network destinations, and external tools, because the default live workspace and host integrations cross the microVM boundary by design.

Texans, data-center developers, utilities, and model buyers need public commitments on grid cost, generation, water, community impact, and incentives to become project-level measurements with named accountability.

concepts_taught: content provenance as two distinct mechanisms: a text watermark that may survive some edits but lacks a published detector, versus C2PA metadata whose signed manifest and cryptographic content binding provide tamper evidence but can be stripped

Docker Sandboxes' five-layer boundary model: hypervisor, network proxy, private Docker engine, workspace mode, and credential proxy, plus the shared-skills and host-MCP exceptions that remain outside full microVM isolation
